claims.claim: Advertising is paid communication that promotes a product, service, or brand and is intended to reach an audience.

Advertising revenue funds much of the media system: historically it let newspapers, magazines, and broadcasters cover costs and sell cheaply, and today many free online services and apps are supported by advertising.

Commonly named advertising persuasion techniques include emotional appeals, celebrity endorsement, bandwagon appeals, fear appeals, humor, and repetition; these are standard descriptive categories in media-literacy and advertising vocabulary.

Celebrity endorsement is a long-standing technique (film-star testimonials date to the 1920s), and U.S. endorsement norms treat endorsements as advertising that should reflect honest opinion and disclose unexpected material connections between endorser and brand.

Advertisers divide audiences into segments and target messages at chosen segments; demographic segmentation sorts by observable characteristics such as age, gender, income, education, occupation, and family structure, while psychographic segmentation sorts by lifestyle, personality, and values.

Digital platforms can personalize the advertising a person sees based on signals such as searches, viewing, and clicks, so advertisers can reach narrowly defined groups; this data-informed targeting raises privacy questions that remain the subject of debate and policy.
Product placement integrates brands into the scenes of shows, films, and games rather than into separate commercials, and has existed since early cinema.

Native advertising is advertising designed to resemble the news, feature articles, reviews, or entertainment content around it; under the FTC Act, when an ad's format could mislead consumers into thinking it is not advertising, a clear and prominent disclosure is necessary, and the more similar the format, the more likely disclosure is required.

Under the U.S. Federal Trade Commission Act, advertising must be truthful and non-deceptive, advertisers must have evidence to back up their claims (substantiation), and advertisements cannot be unfair.

Under the FTC's deception framework, an advertisement is deceptive if it contains a statement or omission likely to mislead consumers acting reasonably under the circumstances and the matter is material, meaning important to a consumer's decision to buy or use the product.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Popular claims about how many advertisements a person sees per day (e.g., 4,000-10,000) are widely repeated but lack a settled basis; OpenStax repeats one such figure while other sources dispute its derivation.
positions: High daily ad-exposure figures are often quoted in marketing texts
The figures trace to unverifiable or contested estimates
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson makes no quantitative claim about ad exposure and avoids the statistic entirely.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether advertising mainly reflects existing culture or actively shapes it is a long-standing debate in media studies.
positions: Advertising simply reflects trends inherent in a culture
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson describes techniques, targeting, funding, and regulation without asserting a one-way cultural effect.

conflictingEvidence.issue: FTC enforcement is case-by-case, so a legal ad is not automatically true, and truth-in-advertising rules differ outside the United States.
positions: U.S. rules require truthfulness, non-deception, and substantiation
Enforcement is complaint- and case-driven and varies by jurisdiction
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson frames the FTC rules as a U.S. baseline, notes case-by-case enforcement, and is explicitly general education rather than legal advice.

sourceRecords.title: Advertising FAQ's: A Guide for Small Business
sourceRecords.notes: Registry record reused (identical id and URL). Re-read live on 2026-08-21. Supports: under the FTC Act advertising must be truthful and non-deceptive, advertisers must have evidence to back up claims, and ads cannot be unfair; substantiation applies to health/safety and other claims; the deception framework (statement or omission likely to mislead consumers acting reasonably, and material to the buying decision); material omissions count. General education only; no legal advice.

sourceRecords.title: FTC's Endorsement Guides: What People Are Asking
sourceRecords.notes: Registry record reused (identical id and URL); verified by a prior worker reading the live page. Supports the high-level treatment of endorsements: endorsements are advertising when there is a material connection, endorsers should give honest opinions, and unexpected material connections should be disclosed. Used only for the endorsement-norms concept; no campaign or disclosure practice is assessed.

sourceRecords.title: Native Advertising: A Guide for Businesses
sourceRecords.notes: Read live on 2026-08-21. New source id (URL not previously registered). Supports: native advertising as content bearing similarity to the news, feature articles, product reviews, entertainment, and other material surrounding it online; the FTC Act prohibition on deceptive or unfair practices applying to native formats; the principle that an ad or promotional message should not suggest it is anything other than an ad; and that when a disclosure is necessary to prevent deception it must be clear and prominent, with the more similar the format the more likely disclosure is needed. Facts only; the guide's examples were read but not reproduced; invented examples used instead.

sourceRecords.title: Understanding Media and Culture, 12.1 Advertising (SUNY OER course version)
sourceRecords.provider: Lumen Learning (course built on the University of Minnesota open textbook)
sourceRecords.notes: Read live on 2026-08-21 (chapter footer confirms CC BY-NC-SA 4.0). Tier B open textbook. Supports: advertising as promoting a product or service through paid announcements; advertising revenue allowing early newspapers to sell cheaply and print independently and funding magazines; radio programming shaped to advertisers' target demographics; 1920s celebrity testimonials/product endorsements in the film industry; product placement from the 1890s (Lumière-era films) through the reality-television boom; the Internet offering free services in exchange for advertising exposure and enabling personally targeted ads, with privacy concerns; the FTC as charged with ensuring advertisements make verifiable claims and do not mislead. Facts synthesized in original prose; the chapter's brand-name examples were not reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Principles of Marketing, Chapter 5: Market Segmentation, Targeting, and Positioning
sourceRecords.notes: Registry record reused (identical id and URL). Section 5.1 was additionally read via an Internet Archive capture of 2024-09-17 to verify details. Supports: segmentation as dividing a market into smaller, more precisely defined groups with common needs expected to respond similarly; geographic (where), demographic (who), behavioral (how), and psychographic (why) segmentation bases; demographic factors (age, gender, income, education, occupation, family structure); psychographic factors (lifestyle, personality variables, values). Facts only; no prose adapted.

sourceRecords.title: Fear appeal
sourceRecords.notes: Tier D reference read via the Wikipedia REST API on 2026-08-21. Supports the general definition of a fear appeal as a term used in psychology, sociology, and marketing for a strategy that motivates action by arousing fear: a persuasive message that attempts to arouse fear through the threat of impending danger or harm and may suggest protective action. Used only to verify the technique name and its general description; no wording reproduced.
